This post is the second in a series following the MIT OCW course *6.041 Probabilistic Systems Analysis and Applied Probability* [@probabilistic-systems-analysis-applied-probability-playlist] and its newer version *6.012 Introduction to Probability* [@intro-to-probability-spring-2018-playlist]. The primary textbook for this series is @bertsekas2008introduction [Sections 1.3–1.4].

# The Question That Drives This Post

Imagine you are an air traffic controller staring at a radar screen. Most of the time, the sky above your sector is empty. But every now and then, an airplane passes through. Your radar is good, but not perfect: it occasionally misses a real plane, and it occasionally fires a false alarm when nothing is there.

One evening, the radar beeps. A blip appears on your screen. You now face a question that matters: **given that the radar registered something, how likely is it that there is actually an airplane overhead?**

Your gut reaction might be: "Well, the radar is pretty accurate, so it's probably a real plane." But as we will see, that gut reaction can be dangerously wrong. The answer depends not just on how good the radar is, but on how rare airplanes are in the first place. Working through this problem carefully will require three tools, each building on the previous one. By the end of this post, you will have all three in hand, and the answer will be both precise and surprising.

# A Quick Review: Probability Axioms

In the [previous post](../probability-models-and-axioms/index.qmd), we set up the foundations of a probability model. Let us briefly recall the key ingredients.

We start by listing all possible outcomes of a random experiment. This list is called the **sample space**, denoted $\Omega$. The outcomes must be mutually exclusive (at most one can occur) and collectively exhaustive (at least one must occur). A subset of $\Omega$ is called an **event**. We then assign probabilities to events according to three axioms [@bertsekas2008introduction, Section 1.2]:

1. **Non-negativity:** For any event $A$, $\mathrm{P}\left(A\right) \geq 0$.
2. **Normalization:** $\mathrm{P}\left(\Omega\right) = 1$.
3. **Countable additivity:** If $A_1, A_2, \dots$ are disjoint events, then

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots\right) = \mathrm{P}\left(A_1\right) + \mathrm{P}\left(A_2\right) + \cdots
$$

That third axiom deserves a moment of attention, because the word *countable* is doing important work. Here is a puzzle that illustrates why.

## The Unit Square Puzzle

Consider the unit square $\Omega = \left[0, 1\right] \times \left[0, 1\right]$, and define the probability of any subset to be its area. Now, the unit square is the union of all of its individual points:

$$
\Omega = \bigcup_{\left(x, y\right) \in \Omega} \left\{\left(x, y\right)\right\}.
$$

Each individual point $\left\{(x,y)\right\}$ has area zero, so $\mathrm{P}\left(\left\{(x,y)\right\}\right) = 0$. If we could apply the additivity axiom here, we would get

$$
1 = \mathrm{P}\left(\Omega\right) = \sum_{\left(x,y\right) \in \Omega} \mathrm{P}\left(\left\{(x,y)\right\}\right) = \sum_{\left(x,y\right) \in \Omega} 0 = 0.
$$

We would have just "proved" that $1 = 0$. Something has gone wrong.

The resolution is that the unit square contains *uncountably* many points. You cannot list them all in a sequence $\left(x_1, y_1\right), \left(x_2, y_2\right), \dots$ and exhaust the entire square; there are simply too many. The additivity axiom only applies to *countable* (i.e., sequenceable) collections of disjoint events. The union above is an uncountable union, so the axiom does not apply, and the "proof" is invalid.

This also leads to an important philosophical observation: in continuous probability models, zero probability does not mean impossible. Every individual point in the unit square has probability zero, yet when you perform the experiment, *some* point will be the outcome. The outcome that actually occurs was, in advance, an event of probability zero. As the lecture puts it: "always expect the unexpected" [@probabilistic-systems-analysis-applied-probability-playlist].

::: {.callout-note title="A note on zero probability" collapse="true"}
Symmetrically, probability one does not mean certain. The event "the outcome is not exactly $(0, 0)$" has probability one (the area of the unit square minus one point is still one), but the outcome *could* be $(0, 0)$. In continuous models, probability one means "almost certain," and probability zero means "almost impossible." These subtleties become important when we study continuous random variables later in the series. For now, we will focus on discrete models where zero probability genuinely means impossible.
:::

With the axioms refreshed, we are ready for the main topic. Here is the central question: what happens to our probabilities when we receive new information about the experiment?

# Conditional Probability: Shrinking the Universe

## The Intuition

Suppose you have set up a probability model for some experiment. You have your sample space $\Omega$, your events, and your probability law. Then, before the experiment concludes, somebody tells you: "I can confirm that the outcome lies inside event $B$." This is partial information. It does not tell you the exact outcome, but it rules out everything outside of $B$.

How should you update your beliefs?

Let us work through a concrete example. Consider a sample space that is divided into three regions with the following probabilities:

    ab -> outside [style=invis]

The sample space $\Omega$ has three regions: one outside $B$ with probability $3/6$, and two inside $B$ with probabilities $2/6$ and $1/6$ respectively. The region inside $B$ where $A$ also occurs (i.e., $A \cap B$) has probability $2/6$, and the region inside $B$ where $A$ does *not* occur (i.e., $A^{\mathsf{c}} \cap B$) has probability $1/6$.

Now, someone tells you that event $B$ has occurred. What changes?

First, the region outside $B$ becomes irrelevant. The outcome is definitely inside $B$, so our new universe is just $B$ itself. Within this new universe, we are certain the outcome is somewhere in $B$, so the conditional probability of $B$ given $B$ must be one:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(B \mid B\right) = 1.
$$

Second, within $B$, we keep the *relative proportions* of the original probabilities. The region $A \cap B$ originally had twice the probability of $A^{\mathsf{c}} \cap B$ (that is, $2/6$ versus $1/6$). After conditioning, we preserve this 2-to-1 ratio. Since the two conditional probabilities must add up to one (they partition $B$), we get:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right) = \frac{2}{3}, \qquad \mathrm{P}\left(A^{\mathsf{c}} \mid B\right) = \frac{1}{3}.
$$

Notice the revision of beliefs. Before we learned that $B$ occurred, the probability of $B$ itself was $\left(2 + 1\right)/6 = 1/2$. After learning that $B$ occurred, it became $1$. The probability of $A$ (within $B$) went from $2/6$ to $2/3$. Information changes probabilities.

## The Definition

The intuitive reasoning above translates directly into a clean formula. To compute the conditional probability of $A$ given $B$, we take the probability mass that $A$ and $B$ share and express it as a fraction of the total probability mass assigned to $B$:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right) = \frac{\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right)}{\mathrm{P}\left(B\right)}.
$$ {#eq-conditional_probability_definition}

Let us verify: $\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right) = 2/6$ and $\mathrm{P}\left(B\right) = 3/6$, so $\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right) = \left(2/6\right) / \left(3/6\right) = 2/3$. This matches our intuitive answer.

::: {.callout-important}
@eq-conditional_probability_definition is only defined when $\mathrm{P}\left(B\right) \neq 0$. If $\mathrm{P}\left(B\right) = 0$, the ratio is undefined, and we say the conditional probability is not defined.
:::

## Conditional Probabilities Are Legitimate Probabilities

One important fact: conditional probabilities, given a specific event $B$ with $\mathrm{P}\left(B\right) > 0$, form a perfectly valid probability law on the sample space. They satisfy all three axioms (non-negativity, normalization, countable additivity). This means every theorem and property that holds for ordinary probabilities also holds for conditional probabilities.

For example, if $A_1$ and $A_2$ are disjoint events and $C$ is any event with $\mathrm{P}\left(C\right) > 0$, then:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(A_1 \cup A_2 \mid C\right) = \mathrm{P}\left(A_1 \mid C\right) + \mathrm{P}\left(A_2 \mid C\right).
$$

This is just the additivity axiom applied in the conditional universe where $C$ is known to have occurred. Conditional probabilities do not "taste or smell any different" from ordinary probabilities, as the lecture puts it [@probabilistic-systems-analysis-applied-probability-playlist]. They are simply a new probability law on the same sample space, tailored to the information that $B$ has occurred.

We now have a way to compute $\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right)$ from the definition. But what if the problem is set up the other way around, and we want to find the probability that *two* things happen together? That is exactly what the multiplication rule gives us. Before we get there, let us solidify the definition with a worked example.

# A Worked Example: Two Dice Rolls

Consider rolling a four-sided die twice. The sample space consists of all pairs $\left(x, y\right)$ where $x$ is the result of the first roll and $y$ is the result of the second roll, with $x, y \in \left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}$. Since the die is fair and the rolls are independent, every pair is equally likely, each with probability $1/16$.

Define the following events:

- $B$: the minimum of the two rolls equals $2$, i.e., $\min\left(X, Y\right) = 2$.
- $M = k$: the maximum of the two rolls equals $k$, i.e., $\max\left(X, Y\right) = k$.

Looking at @fig-die_roll_grid, event $B$ consists of the five red and purple cells: $\left\{\left(2,2\right), \left(2,3\right), \left(2,4\right), \left(3,2\right), \left(4,2\right)\right\}$. These are exactly the pairs where the smaller of the two values is $2$.

**Question 1:** What is $\mathrm{P}\left(M = 1 \mid B\right)$?

For the maximum to equal $1$, both rolls would have to be $1$ or less. But if $\min\left(X, Y\right) = 2$, then at least one roll is $2$, so the maximum is at least $2$. The events $\left\{M = 1\right\}$ and $B$ have no overlap:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(M = 1 \mid B\right) = \frac{\mathrm{P}\left(\left\{M = 1\right\} \cap B\right)}{\mathrm{P}\left(B\right)} = \frac{0}{5/16} = 0.
$$

**Question 2:** What is $\mathrm{P}\left(M = 2 \mid B\right)$?

The event $\left\{M = 2\right\}$ consists of the blue and purple cells in @fig-die_roll_grid: $\left\{\left(1,2\right), \left(2,1\right), \left(2,2\right)\right\}$ (all pairs where the *larger* value is $2$). The intersection with $B$ is just the single purple cell $\left\{\left(2,2\right)\right\}$. Applying @eq-conditional_probability_definition:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(M = 2 \mid B\right) = \frac{\mathrm{P}\left(\left\{M = 2\right\} \cap B\right)}{\mathrm{P}\left(B\right)} = \frac{1/16}{5/16} = \frac{1}{5}.
$$

There is a useful shortcut here. Since all $16$ outcomes in the original sample space were equally likely, conditioning on $B$ gives us a *uniform distribution on the five outcomes in $B$*. (Conditioning preserves relative proportions, and all proportions were equal.) So each of the five outcomes in $B$ has conditional probability $1/5$, and we can read off the answer directly: only one of the five outcomes in $B$ has $M = 2$, so the conditional probability is $1/5$.

::: {.callout-tip title="Shortcut for uniform distributions"}
If the original probability model is uniform (all outcomes equally likely), then conditioning on any event $B$ produces a uniform distribution on the outcomes within $B$. This means the conditional probability of any event $A$ given $B$ is simply the number of outcomes in $A \cap B$ divided by the number of outcomes in $B$.
:::

We have now practiced computing conditional probabilities using the definition. The next natural question is: can we go in the other direction? Instead of computing $\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right)$ from $\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right)$ and $\mathrm{P}\left(B\right)$, can we compute $\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right)$ from $\mathrm{P}\left(A\right)$ and $\mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A\right)$? This is the multiplication rule.

# The Multiplication Rule: Chaining Conditions

## Two Events

Rearranging @eq-conditional_probability_definition gives us a formula for the probability that two events both occur:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right) = \mathrm{P}\left(A\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A\right).
$$ {#eq-multiplication_rule_two_events}

This reads: the probability that both $A$ and $B$ happen equals the probability that $A$ happens, multiplied by the conditional probability that $B$ happens given that $A$ has already happened.

You might wonder: why not write $\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right) = \mathrm{P}\left(B\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right)$ instead? That is equally valid. The roles of $A$ and $B$ are symmetric. Both versions are just rearrangements of the same definition. You pick whichever is more convenient for the problem at hand.

Think of it in terms of frequencies. If you repeat the experiment many times, what fraction of the time do both $A$ and $B$ occur? Well, $A$ occurs in a certain fraction of the experiments. Out of *those* experiments (where $A$ occurred), $B$ also occurs in a further fraction. Multiplying these two fractions gives the overall fraction of experiments where both happen.

## Three Events

What if we want the probability that three events all occur? We can extend the same logic. Suppose events $A$, $B$, and $C$ are defined sequentially (think of stages in a process). Then:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B \cap C\right) = \mathrm{P}\left(A\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(C \mid A \cap B\right).
$$ {#eq-multiplication_rule_three_events}

The proof uses the two-event multiplication rule twice. First, treat $\left(A \cap B\right)$ as a single event and $C$ as the second event:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(\left(A \cap B\right) \cap C\right) = \mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(C \mid A \cap B\right).
$$

Then expand $\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right)$ using @eq-multiplication_rule_two_events:

$$
= \mathrm{P}\left(A\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(C \mid A \cap B\right).
$$

The pattern generalizes to any number of events: you multiply conditional probabilities as you move along the chain, each time conditioning on everything that has already occurred.

This is especially natural when the model is described as a **probability tree**, where each branching point corresponds to a new event, and the probabilities on the branches are conditional probabilities given the path taken so far. To find the probability of reaching any leaf of the tree, you simply multiply the probabilities along the path from root to leaf.

We now have the tool we need to tackle our radar problem. Let us return to it.

# Building a Model from Conditional Probabilities: The Radar Problem

Here is the setup, stated precisely.

**Event $A$:** An airplane is flying above your radar sector. From long experience, you know this occurs with probability $0.05$, so $\mathrm{P}\left(A\right) = 0.05$ and $\mathrm{P}\left(A^{\mathsf{c}}\right) = 0.95$.

**Event $B$:** Your radar registers a blip on the screen. The manufacturer's specifications tell you:

- If a plane *is* present, the radar detects it with probability $0.99$: $\mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A\right) = 0.99$.
- If a plane *is* present, the radar misses it with probability $0.01$: $\mathrm{P}\left(B^{\mathsf{c}} \mid A\right) = 0.01$.
- If no plane is present, the radar fires a false alarm with probability $0.10$: $\mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A^{\mathsf{c}}\right) = 0.10$.
- If no plane is present, the radar stays quiet with probability $0.90$: $\mathrm{P}\left(B^{\mathsf{c}} \mid A^{\mathsf{c}}\right) = 0.90$.

Notice something important about how this model is specified. We are *not* given the overall probability of $B$ directly. Instead, the model is built from *conditional probabilities*: under each scenario (plane present or not), we know how the radar behaves. This is extremely natural. The manufacturer tested the radar under controlled conditions and can tell you "if there is a plane, here is the detection rate" and "if there is no plane, here is the false alarm rate." The manufacturer does not know how often planes fly over *your* particular sector.

This sequential structure is captured beautifully by a probability tree.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-radar_tree
//| fig-cap: "Probability tree for the radar problem. At each branching point, the probabilities on the branches are conditional on the path taken so far. Leaf probabilities are obtained by multiplying along the path."
digraph {
    bgcolor="transparent"
    rankdir=LR
    node [fontcolor="#e6e6e6", style=filled, color="#e6e6e6", fillcolor="#333333", fontname="Helvetica"]
    edge [color="#e6e6e6", fontcolor="#e6e6e6", fontname="Helvetica"]
    graph [fontcolor="#e6e6e6", fontname="Helvetica"]

    start [label="Start", shape=circle, width=0.6, fillcolor="#444444"]

    A [label="A\n(Plane present)", shape=box, fillcolor="#2e86c1"]
    Ac [label="Aᶜ\n(No plane)", shape=box, fillcolor="#1a5276"]

    AB [label="A ∩ B\n(Detected)\n0.0495", shape=box, fillcolor="#27ae60"]
    ABc [label="A ∩ Bᶜ\n(Missed)\n0.0005", shape=box, fillcolor="#555555"]
    AcB [label="Aᶜ ∩ B\n(False alarm)\n0.0950", shape=box, fillcolor="#e67e22"]
    AcBc [label="Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ\n(Quiet)\n0.8550", shape=box, fillcolor="#555555"]

    start -> A [label="  P(A) = 0.05  ", fontsize=12]
    start -> Ac [label="  P(Aᶜ) = 0.95  ", fontsize=12]

    A -> AB [label="  P(B|A) = 0.99  ", fontsize=11]
    A -> ABc [label="  P(Bᶜ|A) = 0.01  ", fontsize=11]

    Ac -> AcB [label="  P(B|Aᶜ) = 0.10  ", fontsize=11]
    Ac -> AcBc [label="  P(Bᶜ|Aᶜ) = 0.90  ", fontsize=11]
}
```

Using the multiplication rule (@eq-multiplication_rule_two_events), we can compute the probability of each leaf:

$$
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right) &= \mathrm{P}\left(A\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A\right) = 0.05 \times 0.99 = 0.0495,\\
    \mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B^{\mathsf{c}}\right) &= \mathrm{P}\left(A\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B^{\mathsf{c}} \mid A\right) = 0.05 \times 0.01 = 0.0005,\\
    \mathrm{P}\left(A^{\mathsf{c}} \cap B\right) &= \mathrm{P}\left(A^{\mathsf{c}}\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A^{\mathsf{c}}\right) = 0.95 \times 0.10 = 0.0950,\\
    \mathrm{P}\left(A^{\mathsf{c}} \cap B^{\mathsf{c}}\right) &= \mathrm{P}\left(A^{\mathsf{c}}\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B^{\mathsf{c}} \mid A^{\mathsf{c}}\right) = 0.95 \times 0.90 = 0.8550.
\end{align*}
$$

You can verify that these four leaf probabilities sum to $1$, as they should (they form a partition of the sample space).

Good. We have computed the probability of each leaf. But the question we really want to answer requires the *total* probability that the radar registers something, regardless of whether a plane is present or not. That is, we need $\mathrm{P}\left(B\right)$. The event $B$ can happen in two ways: via the top branch ($A \cap B$) or via the bottom branch ($A^{\mathsf{c}} \cap B$). How do we combine them?

# The Total Probability Theorem: Divide and Conquer

## The Idea

The event $B$ (the radar beeps) can happen in two mutually exclusive ways: either a plane is present and the radar detects it ($A \cap B$), or no plane is present and the radar fires a false alarm ($A^{\mathsf{c}} \cap B$). Since these two sub-events are disjoint and together they make up all of $B$, we can add their probabilities:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(B\right) = \mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right) + \mathrm{P}\left(A^{\mathsf{c}} \cap B\right).
$$

Substituting the values we computed:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(B\right) = 0.0495 + 0.0950 = 0.1445.
$$

So there is approximately a $14.5\%$ chance that your radar will register a blip on any given occasion.

## The General Statement

The reasoning above generalizes naturally. Suppose the sample space is partitioned into $n$ mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive scenarios $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$ (i.e., exactly one of them occurs). For any event $B$:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(B\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{P}\left(A_i\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A_i\right).
$$ {#eq-total_probability_theorem}

This is the **total probability theorem** [@bertsekas2008introduction, Section 1.3]. It says: to find the overall probability of $B$, consider each possible scenario $A_i$, compute how likely $B$ is under that scenario, and then take a weighted average, where the weights are the probabilities of the scenarios.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-total_probability_partition
//| fig-cap: "The total probability theorem. The sample space is partitioned into scenarios $A_1, A_2, A_3$. Event $B$ cuts across all three. The total probability of $B$ is the sum of the probabilities of $B$ within each scenario."
digraph {
    bgcolor="transparent"
    node [fontcolor="#e6e6e6", style=filled, color="#e6e6e6", fontname="Helvetica"]
    edge [style=invis]
    graph [fontcolor="#e6e6e6", fontname="Helvetica"]

    subgraph cluster_omega {
        label="Ω"
        fontcolor="#e6e6e6"
        fontsize=18
        color="#777777"
        style="dashed"

        subgraph cluster_a1 {
            label="A₁"
            fontcolor="#e6e6e6"
            fontsize=14
            color="#5dade2"
            style="dashed"
            a1b [label="A₁ ∩ B", fillcolor="#2e86c1", shape=box]
            a1nb [label="A₁ ∩ Bᶜ", fillcolor="#1a3c5e", shape=box]
        }

        subgraph cluster_a2 {
            label="A₂"
            fontcolor="#e6e6e6"
            fontsize=14
            color="#e67e22"
            style="dashed"
            a2b [label="A₂ ∩ B", fillcolor="#b35c17", shape=box]
            a2nb [label="A₂ ∩ Bᶜ", fillcolor="#5a3010", shape=box]
        }

        subgraph cluster_a3 {
            label="A₃"
            fontcolor="#e6e6e6"
            fontsize=14
            color="#27ae60"
            style="dashed"
            a3b [label="A₃ ∩ B", fillcolor="#1e8449", shape=box]
            a3nb [label="A₃ ∩ Bᶜ", fillcolor="#0e3d22", shape=box]
        }
    }
}
```

You might notice that @eq-total_probability_theorem is a *weighted average*. The weights are $\mathrm{P}\left(A_1\right), \mathrm{P}\left(A_2\right), \dots, \mathrm{P}\left(A_n\right)$, which sum to one because the $A_i$'s partition $\Omega$. In the special case where all scenarios are equally likely, the total probability of $B$ is simply the *arithmetic* average of the conditional probabilities $\mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A_i\right)$.

The total probability theorem is a "divide and conquer" strategy. If computing $\mathrm{P}\left(B\right)$ directly is hard, break the problem into scenarios where it is easy, compute $\mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A_i\right)$ in each scenario, and then combine.

Let us take stock. We now have two of our three tools: the multiplication rule (for computing joint probabilities by chaining conditions along a tree) and the total probability theorem (for computing marginal probabilities by summing over scenarios). There is one question left: the one we started with. Given that the radar beeped, how likely is it that there is actually a plane overhead? To answer it, we need to *reverse the direction of conditioning*. We know $\mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A\right)$ (the probability of a radar blip given a plane), and we want $\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right)$ (the probability of a plane given a radar blip). This reversal is Bayes' rule.

# Bayes' Rule: Reversing the Arrow

## The Derivation

We want $\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right)$. By the definition of conditional probability:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right) = \frac{\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right)}{\mathrm{P}\left(B\right)}.
$$

We already computed both the numerator and the denominator for the radar problem. The numerator is $\mathrm{P}\left(A \cap B\right) = 0.0495$ (from the multiplication rule), and the denominator is $\mathrm{P}\left(B\right) = 0.1445$ (from the total probability theorem). So:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right) = \frac{0.0495}{0.1445} \approx 0.3426.
$$

Given that the radar registered a blip, there is only about a **34%** chance that an airplane is actually present.

## Why Is This So Low?

This result is surprising. The radar has a $99\%$ detection rate and only a $10\%$ false alarm rate. Those sound like excellent specs. So why is the conditional probability of a plane, given a blip, only $34\%$?

The key is the **base rate**. Airplanes are rare: only $5\%$ of the time is there a plane overhead. Most of the time ($95\%$), the sky is empty. Even though the false alarm rate is "only" $10\%$, that $10\%$ is applied to the $95\%$ of experiments where no plane is present. In absolute terms:

- The probability of a true detection (plane present and radar beeps) is $0.05 \times 0.99 = 0.0495$.
- The probability of a false alarm (no plane but radar beeps) is $0.95 \times 0.10 = 0.0950$.

False alarms are roughly twice as likely as true detections. So when the radar beeps, it is actually more likely to be a false alarm than a real plane. The rarity of the underlying event (the "prior" probability) overwhelms the accuracy of the measuring device.

::: {.callout-note title="The base rate fallacy in medicine" collapse="true"}
This exact reasoning applies to medical testing. Suppose a disease affects $1$ in $1{,}000$ people, and a diagnostic test has a $99\%$ detection rate with a $5\%$ false positive rate. If you test positive, a naive reading might suggest you almost certainly have the disease. But applying Bayes' rule, the probability is only about $2\%$. The overwhelming majority of positive results are false positives, simply because the disease is so rare. This is known as the **base rate fallacy**, and it is a common source of misinterpretation in medical testing, legal reasoning, and everyday life.
:::

## The General Formula

In the general setting, suppose the sample space is partitioned into scenarios $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$. We are given the *prior* probabilities $\mathrm{P}\left(A_i\right)$ (our initial beliefs about which scenario is true) and the *likelihoods* $\mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A_i\right)$ (how likely the observation $B$ is under each scenario). After observing that $B$ has occurred, we compute the *posterior* probability of each scenario:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(A_i \mid B\right) = \frac{\mathrm{P}\left(A_i\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A_i\right)}{\mathrm{P}\left(B\right)} = \frac{\mathrm{P}\left(A_i\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A_i\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n} \mathrm{P}\left(A_j\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(B \mid A_j\right)}.
$$ {#eq-bayes_rule}

This is **Bayes' rule** [@bertsekas2008introduction, Section 1.4]. The denominator is just the total probability theorem (@eq-total_probability_theorem), ensuring that the posterior probabilities sum to one across all scenarios.

## The Conceptual Picture: Cause and Effect, Reversed

Bayes' rule performs a fundamental logical operation: it reverses the direction of reasoning. In many real-world problems, we have a *causal model* that runs in one direction:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-align: center
flowchart LR
    A["<b>Cause</b><br/>(Scenario Aᵢ)"] -->|"P(B | Aᵢ)<br/>Causal model"| B["<b>Effect</b><br/>(Observation B)"]
    B -->|"P(Aᵢ | B)<br/>Inference (Bayes' rule)"| A
```

We know the cause-to-effect direction: given the scenario, how likely is the observation? This is what the manufacturer's specs tell us. But we *observe* the effect and want to *infer* the cause. Bayes' rule provides the precise formula for this inference.

The rule is named after Thomas Bayes, an 18th-century British minister and mathematician who sought a systematic method for updating beliefs in light of new evidence. His work, published posthumously in 1763, laid the foundation for what we now call Bayesian inference, which is one of the most powerful frameworks in all of statistics, machine learning, and decision-making [@bertsekas2008introduction].

# The Big Picture: Three Tools, One Toolkit

Let us step back and see what we have built. Starting from the single definition of conditional probability, we derived three tools.

<!-- big picture mermaid -->

The **multiplication rule** lets us compute joint probabilities by walking along the branches of a tree and multiplying. The **total probability theorem** lets us compute the overall probability of an event by dividing the problem into scenarios and combining. **Bayes' rule** combines both of these to reverse the direction of conditioning: given an observation, it tells us which scenario most likely produced it.

Let us return to where we started. You are the air traffic controller. The radar beeps. Before the beep, your belief that a plane was overhead was $5\%$. After the beep, Bayes' rule tells you that your revised belief should be $34\%$. The radar gave you information, and your probability went up substantially (from $5\%$ to $34\%$), but it is still far from certainty. A single radar reading, even from a good radar, is not enough to be confident when planes are rare.

What would make the posterior probability higher? Either a higher base rate (planes are more common in your sector) or a lower false alarm rate (the radar is better at staying quiet when nothing is there). Both of these can be explored quantitatively using @eq-bayes_rule.

In the next post, we will explore **independence**, which is the special case where learning that $B$ occurred tells you absolutely nothing new about $A$, meaning $\mathrm{P}\left(A \mid B\right) = \mathrm{P}\left(A\right)$. Independence simplifies many calculations dramatically and is one of the most important structural assumptions in probability and statistics.
